column9: stem
column28: explanation
column29: hint

column9: Match each word to its meaning.
column14: Classification :: Organizing or grouping things based on similarities
column15: Taxa :: The ranked groups that living things are sorted into
column16: Dichotomous key :: A tool used to help identify an organism
column17: Morphology :: An organism's physical traits and structure
column18: Latin :: The language used for scientific names
column28: Classification is grouping things by their similarities. Taxa (singular: taxon) are the ranked groups, like kingdom or genus. A dichotomous key is a tool for identifying organisms. Morphology means physical traits and structure. Scientific names are written in Latin.
column29: Look for the clue in each meaning: grouping, ranked groups, identify, physical traits, language.

column9: Which choice best describes **taxonomy**?
column14: The study of how organisms interact with their environment
column15: The branch of biology that classifies and names organisms
column16: The practice of preserving and stuffing dead animals
column17: The study of how traits pass from parents to offspring
column28: Taxonomy is the branch of biology that classifies and names organisms based on their characteristics. Interactions with the environment is ecology, preserving animals is taxidermy (a look-alike word), and passing on traits is genetics.
column29: Don't be fooled by a word that only sounds like taxonomy. Taxonomy comes from the Greek word taxis, meaning "arrangement."

column9: Which scientist developed the classification system that is still the basis for modern classification?
column28: Carl Linnaeus built his system in the 1700s and gave us two-part scientific names. Darwin is known for evolution by natural selection, Mendel for genetics with pea plants, and Hooke for naming cells.
column29: This scientist is also the one who gave every species a two-part Latin name.

column9: Species is the broadest (largest) level of classification.
column28: False. Species is the most specific (smallest) level. Kingdom is the broadest.
column29: Think about which level holds only one kind of organism and which one holds millions.

column9: In **binomial nomenclature**, every species gets a scientific name made of ___ words.
column28: Binomial means "two names." Every scientific name has exactly two words, like *Ursus maritimus* for the polar bear.
column29: The prefix bi- means the same thing here that it means in bicycle and binoculars.

column9: The gray wolf's scientific name is *Canis lupus*. What does the first word, *Canis*, name?
column28: The first word of a scientific name is always the genus, a group of similar species. The second word (*lupus*) is the species. Kingdom and family are broader levels that are not part of the name, and "gray wolf" is the common name.
column29: A scientific name is made from the two most specific levels of classification.

column9: Which shows the correct way to write the scientific name for the house cat?
column28: The genus (*Felis*) is always capitalized, and the species (*catus*) is always lowercase. Choices with both words capitalized, both words lowercase, or the capitals flipped break the rule.
column29: One word gets a capital letter and one does not. Which word comes first?

column9: Six of the seven levels of classification are listed (genus is left out). Put them in order from **broadest** to **most specific**.
column28: From broadest to most specific: Kingdom, Phylum, Class, Order, Family, (Genus), Species. Each level fits inside the one before it.
column29: Start with the level that holds millions of very different organisms and end with the level that is just one kind of organism. Use the mnemonic you learned in class.

column9: Which list shows the six kingdoms we use today?
column14: Animalia, Plantae, Fungi, Protista, Monera, Virus
column15: Animalia, Plantae, Fungi, Protista, Eubacteria, Archaebacteria
column16: Animalia, Plantae, Fungi, Monera, Eubacteria, Archaebacteria
column17: Animalia, Plantae, Protista, Bacteria, Virus, Monera
column28: The six kingdoms are Animalia, Plantae, Fungi, Protista, Eubacteria, and Archaebacteria. Monera was the old single kingdom for all bacteria; it was split into Eubacteria and Archaebacteria. Viruses are not placed in any kingdom.
column29: Two of the six kingdoms are bacteria. One old kingdom name was replaced by those two.

column9: The word **dichotomous** means divided into ___ parts.
column28: Dichotomous means "divided into two parts." Each step of a dichotomous key gives you two choices, and you pick the one that fits your organism.
column29: Think about how many choices each numbered step of the fish key gave you.

column9: When you **handwrite** a scientific name, you should underline it.
column28: True. Scientific names are italicized when typed or printed and underlined when handwritten, because you can't write in italics with a pencil.
column29: You can't easily write in italics by hand. What do you do instead?

column9: Why are scientific names written in Latin?
column14: Latin is no longer used in everyday life, so its words don't change
column15: Most scientists today speak Latin as their first language
column16: Latin words are shorter and easier to spell than English words
column17: Latin names tell exactly where each organism was discovered
column28: Latin is no longer used in everyday life, so its words don't change over time, and scientists in every country use the same name. Nobody speaks Latin as a first language today, its words are not shorter or easier, and scientific names don't tell where an organism was found.
column29: Living languages pick up new words and meanings every year. What is different about Latin?

column9: The classification system developed in the 1700s, which modern classification is still based on, grouped organisms by what?
column15: Similarities in their DNA and proteins
column16: The habitats where the organisms lived
column17: What each organism ate and hunted
column28: In the 1700s, organisms were grouped by physical traits and structural differences (how they look and how they are built). Comparing DNA wasn't possible until the 1900s, and habitat or diet alone would group very different organisms together, like a duck and a fish that both live in a pond.
column29: DNA hadn't been studied yet. What could scientists in the 1700s observe just by looking?

column9: Match each organism to its kingdom.
column28: A mushroom is a fungus (absorbs nutrients and doesn't move). An oak tree is a plant (multicellular and photosynthetic). An amoeba is a single eukaryotic cell with no organ systems, so it is a protist. *E. coli* is a common bacterium, a eubacterium. An earthworm is a multicellular heterotroph with no cell walls, an animal.
column29: Ask about each one: Does it have a nucleus? Does it make its own food? Is it one cell or many?

column9: Which level of classification comes right between **Order** and **Genus**?
column28: From broadest to most specific: Kingdom, Phylum, Class, Order, Family, Genus, Species. Family sits between Order and Genus. Class and Phylum are broader than Order, and Species is more specific than Genus.
column29: Say the seven levels in order with your mnemonic, and find Order. Which level comes next?

column9: Which of these groups would contain organisms that are the **most** similar to each other?
column28: The smaller the taxon, the more alike its members are. A genus holds a few closely related species, while a kingdom holds millions of very different organisms. Class and order are in between.
column29: The bigger the taxon, the less similarity. Which choice is the smallest group?

column9: Which kinds of evidence do taxonomists use to classify organisms today? Select all that apply.
column28: Taxonomists use morphology, genetics (DNA similarity), and behavior/ecology to show how organisms are related. How useful an organism is to people says nothing about its relatives, and common names change from place to place, which is why scientific names exist.
column29: Pick the evidence that tells you something about the organism itself, not about the people who named it.

column9: What is the main goal of the way taxonomists classify organisms today?
column15: To group organisms that live in the same habitat
column16: To give every organism one short common name
column17: To group organisms only by their size and color
column28: The goal is to reflect evolutionary relationships, called phylogeny: organisms in the same group share a common ancestor. Habitat, size, and color can be shared by unrelated organisms, and common names are exactly what scientific names replace.
column29: Modern classification uses DNA evidence. What does comparing DNA tell you about two organisms?

column9: Visitors at a bird feeder call the same bird a "house sparrow," a "gorrión," a "musch," and a "hussparf." How do scientists make sure everyone knows they mean the same bird?
column14: They all use the English name, since it is the most common
column15: They all use one scientific name, *Passer domesticus*
column16: They describe the bird's color and size instead of naming it
column17: They use the name from the country where it was first seen
column28: Common names change with language and culture and can be misleading. Scientists everywhere use one Latin scientific name, *Passer domesticus*, so there is no confusion. English isn't everyone's language, and descriptions or local names still differ from place to place.
column29: What kind of name stays the same in every country and every language?

column9: Which shows the American black bear's scientific name written correctly in a **printed** textbook?
column28: In print, a scientific name is italicized, the genus is capitalized, and the species is lowercase: *Ursus americanus*. The choices in plain (not slanted) type are not italicized, and the others break the capital-letter rule.
column29: Check three things: slanted (italic) letters, a capital on the first word, and a lowercase second word.

column9:
Use the list to decide which two animals are most closely related.
Gray wolf: family Canidae, genus *Canis*
Coyote: family Canidae, genus *Canis*
Red fox: family Canidae, genus *Vulpes*
Bobcat: family Felidae, genus *Lynx*
column28: The gray wolf and coyote share the same genus (*Canis*), the most specific level shown, so they are the most closely related. The red fox shares only their family, and the bobcat is in a different family altogether.
column29: The more levels two organisms share, the more closely related they are. Which pair matches on the most specific level?

column9: Which kingdoms are made of **prokaryotic** cells (cells with no nucleus)? Select all that apply.
column28: Archaebacteria and Eubacteria are prokaryotes, with no nucleus and no membrane-bound organelles. Protista, Fungi, Plantae, and Animalia are all eukaryotic and have a nucleus.
column29: Prokaryotes are the smallest, simplest cells. Which kingdoms hold the simplest organisms?

column9: Mystery organism: I am multicellular, with tissues and organs like roots, stems, and leaves. I make my own food by photosynthesis, my cells have walls made of cellulose, and I can't move from place to place. Which kingdom am I in?
column28: Multicellular photosynthetic autotrophs with tissues and organs and cellulose cell walls are Plantae. Some protists, like seaweeds, are also multicellular and photosynthetic, but protists lack complex organ systems such as roots, stems, and leaves. Fungi also can't move, but they absorb nutrients instead of making food, and animals have no cell walls.
column29: Two of these kingdoms have members that make food by photosynthesis. Which of those two has true tissues and organs?

column9: Mystery organism: I live in a pond. I am a single cell with a nucleus, and I use sunlight to make my own food. I have no organ systems. Which kingdom am I in?
column28: A single cell with a nucleus that makes its own food fits Protista: eukaryotes that lack complex organ systems and can be autotrophs or heterotrophs. Bacteria have no nucleus, and plants are multicellular.
column29: Having a nucleus rules out two choices. Which remaining kingdom can be just one cell?

column9: Mystery organism: I grow on a rotting log. My cells have a nucleus, I can't move, and I absorb nutrients from the dead wood. I reproduce by making spores. Which kingdom am I in?
column28: Fungi are non-moving heterotrophs that absorb nutrients from organic matter like dead wood, and many reproduce with spores. Plants make their own food, animals eat their food and most can move, and bacteria have no nucleus.
column29: This organism doesn't make its own food and doesn't move. Which kingdom acts like a recycler of dead things?

column9: Scientists find a single-celled organism with no nucleus living in a boiling hot spring in Yellowstone National Park. It most likely belongs to Kingdom ___.
column28: No nucleus means it is a prokaryote, and an extreme environment like a boiling hot spring points to Archaebacteria (the ancient bacteria). Eubacteria are prokaryotes too, but they are the common bacteria found in soil and on everyday surfaces.
column29: There are two kingdoms of prokaryotes. Which one is known for extreme environments?

column9:
Use the key to identify Sofia's tree. Its leaves are broad and flat, with **rounded** lobes.
1a. Leaves are needles ... go to 2
1b. Leaves are broad and flat ... go to 3
2a. Needles in bundles of five ... White pine
2b. Needles in bundles of two ... Red pine
3a. Leaves have lobes ... go to 4
3b. Leaves have no lobes ... Paper birch
4a. Lobes are rounded ... White oak
4b. Lobes are pointed ... Sugar maple
column28: Path: 1b (broad, flat leaves) → 3a (lobes) → 4a (rounded lobes) → White oak. The sugar maple also has lobes, but they are pointed, and the paper birch has no lobes.
column29: Start at step 1 and follow the "go to" numbers. Read both choices at every step.

column9: You must already know an organism's name before you can use a dichotomous key.
column28: False. A dichotomous key is a tool to help identify an unknown organism. You observe its traits, pick one choice at each step, and the key gives you the name at the end.
column29: Think about the fish lab. Did you know the fish names before you started?

column9: On his handwritten lab report, Diego wrote the eastern white pine's name as **Pinus Strobus** and did not underline it. What should he fix?
column14: Make the second word lowercase and underline the whole name
column15: Make the first word lowercase and put the name in quotation marks
column16: Write the English name instead of the Latin name
column17: Capitalize every letter so the name stands out
column28: The genus (Pinus) stays capitalized, the species (strobus) must be lowercase, and a handwritten scientific name is underlined. Quotation marks, English names, and all capitals are not part of the rules.
column29: Check two rules: which word gets a capital letter, and what you do instead of italics when writing by hand.

column9: The second word in a scientific name, the species name, usually...
column14: names the scientist who discovered the organism
column15: describes a characteristic of the organism
column16: tells which kingdom the organism is in
column17: is capitalized to show that it is important
column28: The species name is always lowercase and usually describes a characteristic of the organism. For example, the polar bear is *Ursus maritimus*, and *maritimus* means "of the sea." It doesn't name the kingdom. Some species names honor a person, but scientists don't name species after themselves, and most species names describe a trait.
column29: The polar bear is *Ursus maritimus*, and *maritimus* means "of the sea." What is that word doing?

column9: Put the six kingdoms in order from **fewest** known species to **most** known species.
column28: Archaebacteria (a couple hundred), Eubacteria (over 10,000), Protista (over 43,000), Fungi (over 100,000), Plantae (nearly 400,000), Animalia (over 1,000,000).
column29: The two prokaryote kingdoms have the fewest known species. Insects alone make one kingdom huge.

column9: Which difference best separates Kingdom Animalia from Kingdom Plantae?
column14: Animals are prokaryotic cells, and plants are eukaryotic cells
column15: Animals are unicellular organisms, and plants are multicellular
column16: Animals lack cell walls and eat; plants have cell walls and make food
column17: Animals are made of cells, and plants are made of tissues instead
column28: Both kingdoms are multicellular eukaryotes made of cells. The real difference is that animals are heterotrophs with no cell walls, while plants are photosynthetic autotrophs with cellulose cell walls.
column29: Both kingdoms are multicellular and eukaryotic. Think about cell walls and food.

column9: The fish dichotomous key uses these words. Match each word to its meaning.
column28: From the fish lab: ventral means the belly side, anterior means the head end, posterior means the tail end, the caudal fin is the tail fin, and barbels are whiskers (like on a catfish).
column29: Anterior and posterior are opposites. Catfish are famous for the last one.

column9: Which kingdoms include organisms that can be either unicellular or multicellular? Select all that apply.
column28: Protista and Fungi each include both unicellular and multicellular organisms (yeast is a single-celled fungus, and a mushroom is a multicellular one). Plants and animals are always multicellular, and bacteria are unicellular.
column29: Think about which kingdoms have both tiny one-celled members you'd need a microscope to see and large many-celled members you can see easily.

column9:
Kit's dichotomous key says:
3a. Has feathers ... go to 5
3b. Has fur ... go to 6
Her animal has fur. She should go to step ___.
column28: Kit picks 3b because her animal has fur, and 3b says go to 6. She skips step 5, which is only for animals with feathers.
column29: Find the statement that matches the animal, then read the number at the end of that line.

column9:
The list shows the most specific level each animal shares with the gray squirrel.
House mouse: order
Fox squirrel: genus
White-tailed deer: class
Eastern chipmunk: family
Put the animals in order from **most** closely related to **least** closely related to the gray squirrel.
column28: Sharing a more specific level means a closer relationship. Fox squirrel (same genus) → eastern chipmunk (same family) → house mouse (same order) → white-tailed deer (same class only).
column29: Line up the four levels from most specific to broadest before you place the animals.

column9: Humans (*Homo sapiens*) and chimpanzees (*Pan troglodytes*) are in the same family but different genera. Humans and ring-tailed lemurs are in the same order but different families. Which statement **must** be true?
column14: Humans are more closely related to lemurs than to chimpanzees
column15: Chimpanzees and lemurs are in the same order
column16: Chimpanzees and lemurs are in the same family
column17: Humans and lemurs share more levels than humans and chimpanzees
column28: Chimpanzees are in the human family, so they are also in the human order. Lemurs are in that same order, so chimpanzees and lemurs share an order. Lemurs are in a different family from humans, so they can't be in the chimpanzees' family. Humans share more levels with chimpanzees (down to family) than with lemurs (down to order).
column29: If two organisms share a family, they also share every broader level above it. Try sketching the groups as circles inside circles.

column9:
Marcus's fish has separate fins, whiskers around its mouth, and a deeply forked tail fin. Use the key to identify it and its path.
1a. Body long and snakelike; fins joined into one ... American eel
1b. Body not snakelike; fins separate ... go to 2
2a. Barbels present ... go to 3
2b. No barbels ... go to 4
3a. Caudal fin deeply forked ... Channel catfish
3b. Caudal fin rounded or square ... Bullhead
4a. Two separate dorsal fins ... Walleye
4b. One dorsal fin ... Northern pike
column28: Separate fins (1b), whiskers are barbels (2a), and a deeply forked tail fin is a forked caudal fin (3a): Channel catfish, path 1b → 2a → 3a. The bullhead has a rounded or square tail, and the path through 2b is only for fish without barbels, so it can't reach a catfish.
column29: Some key words are fish-lab vocabulary. What are whiskers called, and which fin is the tail fin?

column9:
An organism's cells have a nucleus. It does not make its own food, absorbs nutrients from dead leaves, and cannot move. Use the key to find its path.
1a. Cells have no nucleus ... go to 2
1b. Cells have a nucleus ... go to 3
2a. Lives in extreme environments ... Archaebacteria
2b. Lives in common places like soil ... Eubacteria
3a. Makes its own food by photosynthesis ... go to 4
3b. Does not make its own food ... go to 5
4a. Multicellular with tissues and organs ... Plantae
4b. Lacks complex organ systems ... Protista
5a. Absorbs nutrients and cannot move ... Fungi
5b. Eats food and most can move ... Animalia
column28: It has a nucleus (1b), doesn't make its own food (3b), and absorbs nutrients without moving (5a): Fungi. Step 5b is for animals, which eat food and most can move, and 1a is only for cells with no nucleus.
column29: Answer one question at a time: Nucleus? Makes its own food? Absorbs or eats?

column9:
Noah is making a dichotomous key for the class pets. His first step is:
1a. The animal is cute ... go to 2
1b. The animal is not cute ... go to 3
What is the biggest problem with this step?
column14: Step 1 should describe where each pet lives instead of how it looks
column15: "Cute" is an opinion, so different people would choose differently
column16: Step 1 should sort the pets by their names in alphabetical order
column17: Both choices in step 1 should send you to the same next step
column28: Good keys use traits anyone can observe the same way, like "has fur" or "has scales." "Cute" is an opinion, so two students could take different paths for the same pet. Pet names say nothing about the animal's traits, habitat isn't what makes this step fail, and if both choices led to the same step the key couldn't split the pets into groups.
column29: Would you and a friend always pick the same choice for the same animal?

column9: Ava needs a first step for a key that will split these four animals into two groups of two: bald eagle, American robin, walleye, bluegill. Which first step works best?
column14: 1a. Has feathers / 1b. Has scales and fins
column15: 1a. Is a bird / 1b. Has a backbone
column17: 1a. Lives in Wisconsin / 1b. Does not live in Wisconsin
column28: Feathers vs. scales and fins is easy to observe and splits the birds (eagle, robin) from the fish (walleye, bluegill). All four animals have backbones, so "is a bird / has a backbone" isn't a true either-or. "Large/small" is an opinion, and all four live in Wisconsin.
column29: The two choices in a step must be opposites, and each animal should fit only one of them.

column9: If two organisms are in the same class, they must also be in the same order.
column28: False. Order is more specific than class, so one class holds many orders. Sharing a class means sharing the broader levels above it (phylum and kingdom), not the narrower levels below it. A house cat and a white-tailed deer are both in class Mammalia but are in different orders.
column29: Is an order a bigger group or a smaller group than a class?

column9: The muskellunge, Wisconsin's state fish, is *Esox masquinongy*. The northern pike is *Esox lucius*, and the walleye is *Sander vitreus*. Which statement do these names support?
column14: The muskellunge and walleye share a genus, so they are closest
column15: The muskellunge and northern pike are the most closely related pair
column16: The northern pike and the walleye belong to the same species
column17: The walleye is more closely related to the muskellunge than the pike is
column28: The muskellunge and northern pike share the genus *Esox*, so they are each other's closest relatives here. The walleye is in a different genus (*Sander*), and the pike and walleye have different names, so they are different species.
column29: Compare the first word of each name. What does a shared first word tell you?

column9: White-tailed deer: *Odocoileus virginianus*, family Cervidae. Moose: *Alces alces*, family Cervidae. What is the most specific level of classification these two animals share? ___
column20: family|the family|family level|the family level|family cervidae|the family cervidae|cervidae family|cervidae
column28: Their genus names are different (*Odocoileus* and *Alces*), so they don't share a genus or a species. They are both in family Cervidae, so family is the most specific level they share.
column29: Look at the first word of each scientific name before you look at the family.

column9: Long ago, some people grouped whales with fish because they live in water and have fins. Today whales are classified as mammals. Which evidence best supports today's classification?
column14: Whales have fins and a streamlined body shaped like a fish's
column15: Whales spend their whole lives swimming in the ocean like sharks
column16: Whales hunt and eat fish, squid, and other sea animals
column17: Whales have lungs and milk glands and share DNA with mammals
column28: Taxonomists use morphology (lungs, mammary glands that make milk), genetics (DNA similarity), and behavior (nursing their young) to show evolutionary relationships. Fins and a streamlined body, an ocean habitat, and a diet of sea animals can be shared by unrelated animals that live the same way, which is why grouping by them misled people before.
column29: Look for evidence that unrelated animals wouldn't share just by living in the same place.

column9: Ana collects three samples. Sample A: single cells with no nucleus from a salt lake ten times saltier than the ocean. Sample B: single cells with a nucleus and chloroplasts from a pond. Sample C: single cells with no nucleus and strong cell walls from farm soil. Which choice places all three correctly?
column14: A: Archaebacteria, B: Protista, C: Eubacteria
column15: A: Archaebacteria, B: Plantae, C: Eubacteria
column16: A: Eubacteria, B: Protista, C: Archaebacteria
column17: A: Eubacteria, B: Plantae, C: Archaebacteria
column28: A and C have no nucleus, so they are prokaryotes. A lives in an extreme environment (a very salty lake), which points to Archaebacteria; C lives in ordinary farm soil, which fits Eubacteria. B has a nucleus and chloroplasts but is a single cell, so it is a protist. Plants make food too, but they are always multicellular.
column29: Sort by nucleus first. For the cells with no nucleus, think about where each prokaryote kingdom usually lives. For the one with a nucleus, ask whether plants are ever a single cell.

column9: Ethan says, "Fungi should be in Kingdom Plantae because they don't move and many grow in soil." What is the best evidence **against** Ethan's idea?
column14: Fungi and plants both have cells surrounded by cell walls
column15: Fungi cells and plant cells both have a nucleus inside
column16: Fungi absorb food, but plants make food by photosynthesis
column17: Many fungi grow best in damp, shady places in the forest
column28: Fungi are heterotrophs: they can't make their own food and absorb nutrients from organic matter. Plants are photosynthetic autotrophs, so the two kingdoms get food in completely different ways. The other choices are true, but cell walls and a nucleus are things fungi and plants share (they support Ethan), and where fungi grow doesn't tell you which kingdom they belong in.
column29: Evidence against Ethan has to show a real difference between fungi and plants. Which choice names one?

column9:
Jada finds a backyard critter with clear wings and a long, thin, smooth body. Use the key to identify it and its path.
1a. Has wings ... go to 2
1b. Has no wings ... go to 4
2a. Wings covered in colorful scales ... Monarch butterfly
2b. Wings clear ... go to 3
3a. Body fuzzy with yellow and black stripes ... Honey bee
3b. Body long, thin, and smooth ... Dragonfly
4a. Has six legs ... Ant
4b. Has eight legs ... Spider
column28: Wings (1a), clear wings (2b), long, thin, smooth body (3b): Dragonfly. Step 3a is the fuzzy, striped honey bee, 1b is only for critters without wings, and 2a is for wings covered in colorful scales.
column29: Answer each step using only Jada's description: Wings? What kind? What kind of body?

column9: Two organisms are in the same **order**. Which other levels must they also share? Select all that apply.
column28: An order sits inside a class, which sits inside a phylum, which sits inside a kingdom, so organisms in the same order share all three broader levels. Family and genus are more specific, and one order holds many families and genera.
column29: Sharing a level means sharing every bigger group it sits inside. Which choices are bigger groups than order?

column9: Compare three trees: red maple (*Acer rubrum*), red oak (*Quercus rubra*), and box elder (*Acer negundo*). Which two are most closely related?
column14: Red maple and red oak, because both species names mean "red"
column15: Red oak and box elder, because both are large trees
column16: All three are equally related, because they are all trees
column17: Red maple and box elder, because they share the genus *Acer*
column28: Relationships are shown by shared levels, and a shared genus is the closest. The red maple and box elder share the genus *Acer*, even though their common names don't match. A species name (*rubrum*, *rubra*) is just a description, like "red," and unrelated organisms can share the same species word. Being large trees is a trait many unrelated trees share.
column29: Which word in a scientific name names a group of similar species?
